The [decision table](../choose-a-test.qmd) asks two questions: what's your **goal** (the row), and what **type of data** do you have (the column). This page is about the second question, especially the hardest part of it: is a measurement "[Gaussian](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term}" (normally distributed) enough for the left-hand column?

## Why the shape of your data matters {#why}

The methods in the first column work with **[means](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term}** and [SDs](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term} of the values themselves: [t tests](../glossary.qmd#t-test){.term} and [ANOVA](../glossary.qmd#anova){.term} compare means, and [Pearson correlation](../glossary.qmd#pearson-correlation){.term} measures a straight-line association. They assume roughly [normal](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term} data (for t tests and ANOVA, within each group; for a paired t test, the differences). The tests in the second column ([Mann-Whitney](../glossary.qmd#mann-whitney-test){.term}, [Wilcoxon](../glossary.qmd#wilcoxon-signed-rank-test){.term}, [Kruskal-Wallis](../glossary.qmd#kruskal-wallis-test){.term}, [Spearman](../glossary.qmd#spearman-correlation){.term}) work on **[ranks](../glossary.qmd#rank){.term}**. They don't assume a normal distribution.

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 In plain language
A mean is a fair summary of a bell-shaped pile of numbers. It's a poor summary of a lopsided one: a few very long hospital stays drag the mean far away from what's typical. Tests built on means inherit that problem. [Rank-based tests](../glossary.qmd#nonparametric){.term} only ask "which values are bigger?", so a few extreme values can't dominate.
:::

## Look first: histograms and QQ plots {#look}

Always plot before you test. Here are three [variables](../glossary.qmd#variable){.term} from the practice data: age, length of stay, and the 1-year [PROM](../glossary.qmd#prom){.term} score.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3
library(tidyverse)

cohort   <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
proms    <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
one_year <- proms |> filter(visit == "1yr", !is.na(prom_score))

shapes <- bind_rows(
  tibble(variable = "Age, years",           value = cohort$age),
  tibble(variable = "Length of stay, days", value = cohort$los_days),
  tibble(variable = "1-year PROM score",    value = one_year$prom_score)
)

ggplot(shapes, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free")
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
one_year = proms[(proms["visit"] == "1yr") & proms["prom_score"].notna()]

shapes = {
    "Age, years": cohort["age"],
    "Length of stay, days": cohort["los_days"],
    "1-year PROM score": one_year["prom_score"],
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3))
for ax, (name, values) in zip(axes, shapes.items()):
    ax.hist(values, bins=30)
    ax.set_title(name)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

- **Age** is a fairly [symmetric](../glossary.qmd#symmetric){.term} bell.
- **Length of stay** piles up at 0 and 1 days and has a long tail to the right: **right-skewed**.
- **1-year PROM** piles up against the top of the scale (100), with a tail to the left: a **[ceiling effect](../glossary.qmd#ceiling-effect){.term}**.

A **QQ plot** makes the comparison with a [normal distribution](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term} easier to see. If the data are normal, the points fall on the straight line.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(shapes, aes(sample = value)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free")
```

## Python

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3))
for ax, (name, values) in zip(axes, shapes.items()):
    stats.probplot(values, plot=ax)
    ax.set_title(name)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

How to read them:

- Points **on the line**: close to normal (age).
- Points **curving up at the right end**: right skew (length of stay). The flat steps are the many [ties](../glossary.qmd#ties){.term} at 0, 1 and 2 days.
- Points **flattening at the top**: a ceiling (the PROM). Many patients share the maximum score.

A number for lopsidedness is the **[skewness](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term}**: 0 for a symmetric shape, positive for a tail to the right, negative for a tail to the left.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
skewness <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3

c(age      = skewness(cohort$age),
  los      = skewness(cohort$los_days),
  prom_1yr = skewness(one_year$prom_score))
```

## Python

```{python}
def skewness(x):
    return ((x - x.mean()) ** 3).mean() / x.std() ** 3

print(pd.Series({
    "age": skewness(cohort["age"]),
    "los": skewness(cohort["los_days"]),
    "prom_1yr": skewness(one_year["prom_score"]),
}))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"age": float(skewness(cohort["age"])), "los": float(skewness(cohort["los_days"])),
       "prom_1yr": float(skewness(one_year["prom_score"]))}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(age = skewness(cohort$age), los = skewness(cohort$los_days),
                 prom_1yr = skewness(one_year$prom_score)), reticulate::py$chk)
```

Age: −0.05, practically symmetric. Length of stay: 1.61, a long tail to the right. 1-year PROM score: −0.73, a tail to the left. The numbers say what the [histograms](../glossary.qmd#histogram){.term} showed.

As a rule of thumb, a skewness between −0.5 and 0.5 means a shape close to symmetric, a skewness beyond −1 or 1 means a strongly skewed one, and anything in between is moderately skewed. By that guide, age is close to symmetric, the 1-year PROM score is moderately skewed and length of stay is strongly skewed. The cut-offs are a widely used convention for describing a shape, not a test. Read them next to the plots, and don't lean on the skewness of a small [sample](../glossary.qmd#sample){.term}: a few values can move it across a cut-off.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: skewness functions
Packages define skewness in slightly different ways (`scipy.stats.skew()` and the R package `e1071` each use their own formula), so the third decimal can differ between them. We wrote the formula out by hand in both languages so the numbers match exactly.
:::

## Formal tests: Shapiro-Wilk, and why not to trust it alone {#shapiro}

The **Shapiro-Wilk test** asks: "Could these numbers plausibly come from a [normal distribution](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term}?" A small p-value says that numbers like these would be unusual if they did come from a normal distribution; it is not the probability that they do. It's tempting to let it decide: p < 0.05 → [rank test](../glossary.qmd#nonparametric){.term}, otherwise → [t test](../glossary.qmd#t-test){.term}. That rule fails in both directions.

**It's too sensitive with large samples.** Our 600 ages look like a textbook bell curve, yet:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
shapiro.test(cohort$age)
```

## Python

```{python}
print(stats.shapiro(cohort["age"]))
```
:::

p = 0.001: "not normal". With 600 values the test can detect departures far too small to matter. A t test on these ages would be perfectly fine. The other number, W (`statistic` in Python), is the [test statistic](../glossary.qmd#test-statistic){.term}: 1 would be a perfect fit to the normal curve. You don't report it; read the [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} (`p-value` in R, `pvalue` in Python).

**It's too weak with small samples.** Take just the first 10 patients' 1-year PROM scores, from a [variable](../glossary.qmd#variable){.term} we *know* is [skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term} with a ceiling:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
first_ten <- head(one_year$prom_score, 10)
first_ten
shapiro.test(first_ten)
```

## Python

```{python}
first_ten = one_year["prom_score"].head(10)
print(first_ten.tolist())
print(stats.shapiro(first_ten))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
age_sw = stats.shapiro(cohort["age"])
ten_sw = stats.shapiro(first_ten)
chk = {"age_w": float(age_sw.statistic), "age_p": float(age_sw.pvalue),
       "ten_w": float(ten_sw.statistic), "ten_p": float(ten_sw.pvalue)}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
age_sw <- shapiro.test(cohort$age)
ten_sw <- shapiro.test(first_ten)
check_agree(list(age_w = unname(age_sw$statistic), age_p = age_sw$p.value,
                 ten_w = unname(ten_sw$statistic), ten_p = ten_sw$p.value), reticulate::py$chk)
```

p = 0.173: "no evidence against normality". Ten values simply can't reveal the shape, which is exactly when the shape matters most.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: don't let one p-value choose your test
Decide from the plots, from what you know about the measurement (a [bounded](../glossary.qmd#bounded-scale){.term} score, a count of days), and from the [sample size](../glossary.qmd#sample-size){.term}. Use Shapiro-Wilk as supporting evidence, not as the judge. Then say how you decided in your Methods.
:::

## Check within groups, not the pooled data {#within-groups}

The [normality](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term} [assumption](../glossary.qmd#assumption){.term} is about the data **within each group** (for paired data, the differences between the two measurements of each pair; for [regression models](../glossary.qmd#model){.term}, the **[residuals](../glossary.qmd#residual){.term}**: what's left after the model's prediction). Pooling groups with different centers can make perfectly normal data look non-normal.

Here's an extreme, made-up example: two groups of 200 values, each exactly normal, with [means](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} of 40 and 60 and an [SD](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term} of 5, so 4 standard deviations apart.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
group_a <- qnorm(ppoints(200), mean = 40, sd = 5)   # 200 perfectly normal values
group_b <- qnorm(ppoints(200), mean = 60, sd = 5)

shapiro.test(group_a)$p.value                       # one group alone
shapiro.test(c(group_a, group_b))$p.value           # both groups pooled

ggplot(tibble(value = c(group_a, group_b)), aes(value)) +   # the pooled values: two humps
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)
```

## Python

```{python}
points = (np.arange(1, 201) - 0.5) / 200            # the same probabilities as R's ppoints(200)
group_a = stats.norm.ppf(points, loc=40, scale=5)   # 200 perfectly normal values
group_b = stats.norm.ppf(points, loc=60, scale=5)

print(stats.shapiro(group_a).pvalue)                              # one group alone
print(stats.shapiro(np.concatenate([group_a, group_b])).pvalue)   # both groups pooled

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(np.concatenate([group_a, group_b]), bins=30)              # the pooled values: two humps
plt.show()
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"one": float(stats.shapiro(group_a).pvalue),
       "pooled": float(stats.shapiro(np.concatenate([group_a, group_b])).pvalue)}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(one = shapiro.test(group_a)$p.value,
                 pooled = shapiro.test(c(group_a, group_b))$p.value), reticulate::py$chk)
```

Each group alone passes easily (p ≈ 1). Pooled, p < 0.001: the [histogram](../glossary.qmd#histogram){.term} of the pooled values has two humps, one around 40 and one around 60, which is not what a normal distribution looks like.

The pooled [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} prints as `9.267769e-11`. That is [scientific notation](../glossary.qmd#scientific-notation){.term}: 9.27 × 10⁻¹¹, or 0.0000000000927. For one group alone, R rounds the p-value to 1 and Python prints 0.999999999999995.

In real data the groups are usually much closer together. BMI differs by only about a third of a standard deviation between THA and TKA patients (the [SMD](../glossary.qmd#smd){.term} of 0.33 in [Table 1](02-demographics.qmd#smd)), so pooling barely matters. What you see instead is [Shapiro-Wilk](../glossary.qmd#shapiro-wilk-test){.term}'s verdict bouncing around 0.05 depending on how you slice the same data:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
shapiro.test(cohort$bmi)$p.value                         # pooled

cohort |>
  group_by(procedure) |>
  summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(bmi)$p.value)       # each group on its own

fit <- lm(bmi ~ procedure, data = cohort)                # residual = BMI minus its group's mean
shapiro.test(residuals(fit))$p.value

ggplot(tibble(residual = residuals(fit)), aes(sample = residual)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line()
```

## Python

```{python}
print(stats.shapiro(cohort["bmi"]).pvalue)               # pooled

for procedure, group in cohort.groupby("procedure"):     # each group on its own
    print(procedure, stats.shapiro(group["bmi"]).pvalue)

# residual = BMI minus its group's mean
residuals = cohort["bmi"] - cohort.groupby("procedure")["bmi"].transform("mean")
print(stats.shapiro(residuals).pvalue)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
qq = stats.probplot(residuals, plot=ax)                  # naming the result keeps its numbers out of the output
plt.show()
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"pooled": float(stats.shapiro(cohort["bmi"]).pvalue),
       "residuals": float(stats.shapiro(residuals).pvalue)}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(pooled = shapiro.test(cohort$bmi)$p.value,
                 residuals = shapiro.test(residuals(fit))$p.value), reticulate::py$chk)
```

Pooled p = 0.044, THA alone 0.051, TKA alone 0.124, residuals 0.306: four slices of the same data, on both sides of 0.05, while the [QQ plot](../glossary.qmd#qq-plot){.term} is a near-perfect straight line. That's the lesson of the previous section again: decide from the plots and what you know about the measurement, not from one p-value.

## How much does normality matter? {#robustness}

Less than you might think, once groups are reasonably large. Tests on [means](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} rely on the **average** being [roughly normal](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term}, not on every individual value. Thanks to the *central limit theorem*, averages of about 30 or more values are close to normal even when the values themselves are [skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term}.

A practical guide:

- **About 30 or more per group, moderate skew, no wild outliers:** [t tests](../glossary.qmd#t-test){.term} and [ANOVA](../glossary.qmd#anova){.term} are fine. With very skewed data, the [rank test](../glossary.qmd#nonparametric){.term} is still often the better summary.
- **Strong skew or extreme outliers:** use the rank column.
- **Small groups (under about 15 per group):** plots can't show the shape, and no test has much [power](../glossary.qmd#power){.term}. Choose from what you know about the measurement: the rank column for skewed or [ordinal](../glossary.qmd#ordinal){.term} measures, the Gaussian column for measurements known to be roughly normal. Expect wide [confidence intervals](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} either way.
- **Ordinal scales, or a ceiling or floor:** use the rank column whatever the [sample size](../glossary.qmd#sample-size){.term} (below).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Under the hood: the central limit theorem
If you take many random [samples](../glossary.qmd#sample){.term} of size *n* from almost any [distribution](../glossary.qmd#distribution){.term} and compute each sample's mean, those means form a distribution that gets closer to normal as *n* grows. Its [spread](../glossary.qmd#spread){.term} shrinks in proportion to 1/√n. t tests are built on the distribution of the mean, which is why they tolerate non-normal raw data when *n* is large. "About 30" is a rule of thumb, not a law: the more skewed the data, the larger *n* needs to be.
:::

## Skew, ceilings and transformations {#transform}

A common fix for [right skew](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term} is to analyze the **[logarithm](../glossary.qmd#logarithm){.term}** of the values. For length of stay we have to use log(days + 1), because log(0) doesn't exist.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
c(skew_raw      = skewness(cohort$los_days),
  skew_log      = skewness(log1p(cohort$los_days)),   # log1p(x) = log(1 + x)
  share_zero    = mean(cohort$los_days == 0),
  ceiling_1yr   = mean(one_year$prom_score == 100))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

print(pd.Series({
    "skew_raw": skewness(cohort["los_days"]),
    "skew_log": skewness(np.log1p(cohort["los_days"])),   # log1p(x) = log(1 + x)
    "share_zero": (cohort["los_days"] == 0).mean(),
    "ceiling_1yr": (one_year["prom_score"] == 100).mean(),
}))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"skew_log": float(skewness(np.log1p(cohort["los_days"]))),
       "share_zero": float((cohort["los_days"] == 0).mean()),
       "ceiling_1yr": float((one_year["prom_score"] == 100).mean())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(skew_log = skewness(log1p(cohort$los_days)),
                 share_zero = mean(cohort$los_days == 0),
                 ceiling_1yr = mean(one_year$prom_score == 100)), reticulate::py$chk)
```

The log helps (skewness falls from about 1.6 to 0.6), but nearly half the stays are 0 days (`share_zero`: 0.485, or 48.5%) and no transformation can spread out a pile of identical values. Results on a log scale are also harder to explain ("a 0.3 difference in log(days + 1)"). Here the [rank-based tests](../glossary.qmd#nonparametric){.term} are simpler and more honest.

The same goes for the **[ceiling](../glossary.qmd#ceiling-effect){.term}**: 17% of the patients with a 1-year score reach the maximum (`ceiling_1yr`: 0.17), and no transformation can tell those patients apart. Compare groups with rank-based tests, or report the [proportion](../glossary.qmd#proportion){.term} reaching the ceiling (or a clinically important improvement) as a [yes/no outcome](../glossary.qmd#binary){.term}.

## Ordinal data always go in the rank column {#ordinal}

**Ordinal** data have an order but no fixed spacing: satisfaction from 1 ("very dissatisfied") to 5 ("very satisfied"), ASA class, pain "none / mild / moderate / severe". The step from 4 to 5 isn't necessarily the same size as the step from 1 to 2, so averages are hard to interpret.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
count(cohort, satisfaction_1yr)
```

## Python

```{python}
print(cohort["satisfaction_1yr"].value_counts(dropna=False).sort_index())
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"very_satisfied": float((cohort["satisfaction_1yr"] == 5).sum()),
       "no_answer": float(cohort["satisfaction_1yr"].isna().sum())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(very_satisfied = sum(cohort$satisfaction_1yr == 5, na.rm = TRUE),
                 no_answer = sum(is.na(cohort$satisfaction_1yr))), reticulate::py$chk)
```

250 patients chose 5 ("very satisfied") and 15 chose 1. The last row (`NA` in R, `NaN` in Python) is the 98 patients with no answer; say how many are missing when you report the scale. Python prints the scores as `1.0` to `5.0` because the column has blanks.

Report ordinal data as counts and percentages, or as a [median](../glossary.qmd#median){.term} ([IQR](../glossary.qmd#iqr){.term}), and compare groups with [rank-based tests](../glossary.qmd#nonparametric){.term}. A single [Likert](../glossary.qmd#likert-scale){.term} item, such as satisfaction from 1 to 5, goes in the rank column however many patients you have. Statisticians disagree on this: some accept a [t test](../glossary.qmd#t-test){.term} on such answers when the sample is large enough. This site takes the stricter view. A score that adds up the answers to several such items, as many questionnaires do, is a different matter: decide from its distribution, as in the sections above.

## Paired or unpaired? Matched or unmatched? {#paired}

The decision table's rows also ask whether your groups are **[independent](../glossary.qmd#independence){.term}** or **paired/matched**.

- **Unpaired (independent):** different patients in each group. THA vs TKA; Site A vs Site B; men vs women.
- **Paired:** the same patients measured twice, or natural pairs. Pre-op vs 1-year [PROM](../glossary.qmd#prom){.term} in the same patients; left vs right knee in bilateral patients; two raters measuring the same X-rays.
- **Matched:** each patient in one group has their own match, one or more patients in the other group chosen to resemble them (by age, sex, BMI…). Treat such individually matched pairs or sets like pairs.

**Bilateral patients need care.** In our [cohort](../glossary.qmd#cohort){.term}, 80 patients appear twice, once for each side ([page 2](02-demographics.qmd#setup) counts them). Their two procedures share the same person's age, sex and health, so they are not independent. When both fall in the same comparison group, tests that treat every row as a separate patient are a little overconfident ([p-values](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} too small, [CIs](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} too narrow). Either analyse one procedure per patient (for example, the first), or use methods built for [clustered data](../glossary.qmd#clustered-data){.term}, such as [mixed models](../beyond/16-mixed-models.qmd#bilateral). Say which you did.

Pairing matters because measurements on the same patient are related. A paired analysis uses each patient as their own control, which removes the patient-to-patient variation and usually gives a more [precise](../glossary.qmd#precision){.term} answer. Analyzing paired data as if unpaired is one of the most common mistakes in the literature.

## From your question to a test {#flowchart}

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[What is your goal?] --> B[Describe one group]
  A --> M[Compare one group to a hypothetical value]
  A --> C[Compare groups or measurements]
  A --> D[Association or prediction]
  C --> E{Same patients or matched?}
  E -->|No| F[Unpaired rows]
  E -->|Yes| G[Paired / matched rows]
  B --> H{What type of outcome?}
  M --> H
  F --> H
  G --> H
  D --> H
  H -->|Measurement, roughly normal within groups or, for paired data, the differences| I[Gaussian column]
  H -->|Strongly skewed, piled up at a floor or ceiling, or ordinal| J[Rank column]
  H -->|Yes / no| K[Binomial column]
  H -->|Time until an event| L[Survival column]
```

Then find your row and column in the [decision table](../choose-a-test.qmd). Some worked examples from typical orthopaedic research questions:

| Question | Row | Column | Test |
|------|------|------|------|
| Is the EFAS score at 3 months different with a boot than with a cast? | Two unpaired groups | [Gaussian](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term} | [Unpaired t test](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t) |
| Is pain 6 weeks after the injury different with a boot than with a cast? | Two unpaired groups | [Rank](../glossary.qmd#rank){.term} ([ordinal](../glossary.qmd#ordinal){.term}) | [Mann-Whitney test](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#mann-whitney) |
| Did KOOS JR improve from pre-op to 1 year? | Two [paired](../glossary.qmd#paired){.term} groups | Rank ([ceiling](../glossary.qmd#ceiling-effect){.term}) | [Wilcoxon signed-rank test](../catalog/07-two-paired-groups.qmd#wilcoxon-signed-rank) |
| Does graft failure within 2 years differ between hamstring and BPTB grafts? | Two unpaired groups | Binomial | [Fisher's exact test](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#fisher-chi-square) |
| Does satisfaction differ between surgeons S1, S2 and S3? | Three or more unmatched groups | Rank (ordinal) | [Kruskal-Wallis test](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#kruskal-wallis) |
| Does implant design affect [revision-free survival](../glossary.qmd#survival){.term}? | Three or more unmatched groups | Survival | [Cox regression](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#cox) |

## p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals {#effect-sizes}

Every test on this site reports three things. They answer different questions, and a good Results section gives all three.

- The **effect size** answers *how big?* For example, the difference between two [means](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term}.
- The **95% [confidence interval](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} (CI)** answers *how sure are we about that size?* It's the range of effect sizes compatible with the data. The 95% describes the method, not this one interval: if a study were repeated many times, about 95 of every 100 intervals calculated this way would contain the true effect.
- The **p-value** answers *how surprising would data like these be if there were really no difference at all?* It doesn't measure the size or importance of an effect.

Here's all three for BMI in TKA vs THA, using the [unpaired (Welch's) t test](../glossary.qmd#welch-test){.term} from [page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t). It uses all 600 rows, which include both procedures of the 80 bilateral patients ([see above](#paired)).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
bmi_test <- t.test(bmi ~ procedure, data = cohort)   # Welch's t test (R's default)
bmi_test
tapply(cohort$bmi, cohort$procedure, sd)                             # the SD of BMI in each group

difference <- unname(bmi_test$estimate[2] - bmi_test$estimate[1])   # TKA minus THA
ci <- -rev(bmi_test$conf.int)                                        # flip to TKA minus THA
tibble(mean_tka = unname(bmi_test$estimate[2]), mean_tha = unname(bmi_test$estimate[1]),
       difference = difference, ci_low = ci[1], ci_high = ci[2], p = bmi_test$p.value)
```

## Python

```{python}
tka = cohort.loc[cohort["procedure"] == "TKA", "bmi"]
tha = cohort.loc[cohort["procedure"] == "THA", "bmi"]

bmi_test = stats.ttest_ind(tka, tha, equal_var=False)   # Welch's t test
ci = bmi_test.confidence_interval()
print(cohort.groupby("procedure")["bmi"].std())          # the SD of BMI in each group

print(pd.Series({"mean_tka": tka.mean(), "mean_tha": tha.mean(),
                 "difference": tka.mean() - tha.mean(),
                 "ci_low": ci.low, "ci_high": ci.high, "p": bmi_test.pvalue}))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"mean_tka": float(tka.mean()), "mean_tha": float(tha.mean()),
       "sd_tka": float(tka.std()), "sd_tha": float(tha.std()),
       "difference": float(tka.mean() - tha.mean()), "ci_low": float(ci.low),
       "ci_high": float(ci.high), "p": float(bmi_test.pvalue)}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(mean_tka = unname(bmi_test$estimate[2]), mean_tha = unname(bmi_test$estimate[1]),
                 sd_tka = sd(cohort$bmi[cohort$procedure == "TKA"]), sd_tha = sd(cohort$bmi[cohort$procedure == "THA"]),
                 difference = difference, ci_low = ci[1], ci_high = ci[2], p = bmi_test$p.value),
            reticulate::py$chk)
```

Reading the output: mean BMI is 31.2 for TKA and 29.5 for THA (`mean_tka` and `mean_tha`), with SDs of 5.4 and 5.3 (the line that prints the SD of each group). The difference is 1.786, so 1.8 to one decimal (it comes from the unrounded means, which is why it isn't 31.2 − 29.5 = 1.7). The CI runs from 0.924 to 2.647, so 0.9 to 2.6 (R's small table shows 2.65 because it prints three significant figures). R prints p as `5.341e-05`, which is 0.00005 and is written as p < 0.001. R's first printout also shows t and df, the [test statistic](../glossary.qmd#test-statistic){.term} and its [degrees of freedom](../glossary.qmd#degrees-of-freedom){.term}; [page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t) explains them, and here we need only the two means and SDs, the difference, its CI and p.

> Mean BMI was 31.2 kg/m² (SD 5.4) for TKA and 29.5 kg/m² (SD 5.3) for THA (mean difference 1.8 kg/m², 95% CI 0.9 to 2.6; p < 0.001).

Is a difference of 1.8 kg/m² *clinically* important? The p-value can't tell you. Ask whether a difference anywhere in the CI (0.9 to 2.6 kg/m²) would change risk or management, for example complication rates. That's clinical judgment, not statistics. **Statistically significant** means only that data like these would be unusual if there were really no difference. It doesn't mean the difference is large or important.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: three classic misreadings
- **"p = 0.20, so there's no difference."** No. It means the data couldn't rule out zero. Look at the CI: if it runs from "harmful" to "very helpful", the study was too small to say.
- **"p < 0.001, so the effect is large."** No. With enough patients, tiny differences get tiny p-values. Look at the effect size and CI.
- **"p = 0.03, so there's a 3% chance that there's no difference."** No. The p-value is calculated *assuming* there is no difference, so it can't be the probability that there is none. It says how unusual data like these would be if there were no difference.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: which group comes first
R's `t.test(bmi ~ procedure)` subtracts in alphabetical order of the groups (THA minus TKA). `scipy`'s `ttest_ind(tka, tha)` subtracts the second argument from the first. Same answer, opposite sign. Always say which group was subtracted from which, as we did above.
:::

For [PROMs](../glossary.qmd#prom){.term}, judge differences against the **minimal clinically important difference (MCID)**: the smallest change patients notice as meaningful. Published MCIDs vary with the study and the method used to derive them, so cite the one you use. Be careful how you use it: an MCID is a *within-patient* threshold for one person's change. A difference between two groups' averages that is smaller than the MCID doesn't prove no patient benefited, and a larger one doesn't mean every patient did. Comparing the [proportion](../glossary.qmd#proportion){.term} of patients in each group who reached the MCID is often the clearer analysis.

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  round(shapiro.test(cohort$age)$p.value, 3) == 0.001,
  round(shapiro.test(first_ten)$p.value, 3) == 0.173,

  round(shapiro.test(residuals(fit))$p.value, 3) == 0.306,
  shapiro.test(group_a)$p.value > 0.99,

  # numbers added with the audit fixes
  round(c(skewness(cohort$age), skewness(cohort$los_days), skewness(one_year$prom_score)), 2) == c(-0.05, 1.61, -0.73),
  isTRUE(all.equal(mean(group_a), 40)), isTRUE(all.equal(mean(group_b), 60)), (60 - 40) / 5 == 4,
  format(signif(shapiro.test(c(group_a, group_b))$p.value, 7)) == "9.267769e-11",
  round(shapiro.test(group_a)$p.value, 6) == 1,
  reticulate::py_eval("str(stats.shapiro(group_a).pvalue)") == "0.999999999999995",
  round(abs(smd::smd(cohort$bmi, cohort$procedure)$estimate), 2) == 0.33,
  round(mean(cohort$los_days == 0), 3) == 0.485, round(mean(one_year$prom_score == 100), 2) == 0.17,
  sum(cohort$satisfaction_1yr == 5, na.rm = TRUE) == 250, sum(cohort$satisfaction_1yr == 1, na.rm = TRUE) == 15,

  round(difference, 3) == 1.786, round(ci, 3) == c(0.924, 2.647), format(signif(ci[2], 3)) == "2.65",

  mean(cohort$los_days == 0) > 0.45, mean(cohort$los_days == 0) < 0.5,

  abs(skewness(cohort$age)) < 0.5,
  abs(skewness(one_year$prom_score)) > 0.5, abs(skewness(one_year$prom_score)) < 1,
```

## Exercises {#exercises}

**1.** Draw a [histogram](../glossary.qmd#histogram){.term} and a [QQ plot](../glossary.qmd#qq-plot){.term} of the **pre-op** [PROM](../glossary.qmd#prom){.term} score. Is it closer to [normal](../glossary.qmd#normal-distribution){.term} than the 1-year score? Why might that be?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
preop <- proms |> filter(visit == "preop", !is.na(prom_score))
ggplot(preop, aes(prom_score)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30)
ggplot(preop, aes(sample = prom_score)) + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()
skewness(preop$prom_score)
```

## Python

```{python}
preop = proms[(proms["visit"] == "preop") & proms["prom_score"].notna()]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3))
axes[0].hist(preop["prom_score"], bins=30)
qq = stats.probplot(preop["prom_score"], plot=axes[1])   # naming the result keeps its numbers out of the output
plt.show()
print(skewness(preop["prom_score"]))
```
:::

Much closer to normal: [skewness](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term} about 0.1 and the QQ points follow the line. Before surgery, scores sit in the middle of the scale, far from the ceiling. After a successful operation many patients hit the maximum, which creates the [ceiling](../glossary.qmd#ceiling-effect){.term}.
:::

**2.** A fellow wants to compare operative time between surgeons S1 and S2, about 40 cases each. The histogram is fairly [symmetric](../glossary.qmd#symmetric){.term}, with a few long cases. Which column of the decision table would you use, and how would you justify it in the Methods?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The Gaussian column (an [unpaired t test](../glossary.qmd#t-test){.term}, [Welch's version](../glossary.qmd#welch-test){.term}) is reasonable. With about 40 cases per group and a roughly symmetric shape, the t test is [robust](../glossary.qmd#robust){.term}. Check the QQ plot within each surgeon, and check that the few long cases aren't extreme [outliers](../glossary.qmd#outlier){.term}. Methods: "Operative time was approximately normally distributed within each group on visual inspection of histograms and QQ plots, and was compared with Welch's t test." If the long cases were extreme, a [Mann-Whitney test](../glossary.qmd#mann-whitney-test){.term} would be the safer choice; say so.
:::

**3.** A study reports: "1-year KOOS JR was 2.1 points higher with the new implant (95% CI −1.5 to 5.7; p = 0.25)." Suppose the [MCID](../glossary.qmd#mcid){.term} for KOOS JR is 14 points. Write one sentence interpreting this result.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
"The study found no clear difference in 1-year KOOS JR between implants: the estimate (2.1 points) and the whole 95% CI (−1.5 to 5.7) are far smaller than the 14-point MCID, so a large average benefit of the new implant is unlikely."

This is stronger than "not [significant](../glossary.qmd#statistical-significance){.term}": the [CI](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} rules out a large average difference. Strictly, the MCID is a within-patient threshold, so the clearest follow-up analysis compares the [proportion](../glossary.qmd#proportion){.term} of patients in each group who improved by at least 14 points.
:::
